blocks.content: This topic covers real, practical principles for designing a genuinely well-built module, building directly on the Modules module covered earlier in this course.
1. Recap: The Modules Module
The Modules module already covered what a module is, its structure, and its inputs and outputs, this topic covers the real, practical principles for designing one well.
A module that is mechanically correct can still be genuinely poorly designed, hard to use, hard to extend, or trying to do too much at once.
This topic addresses that gap directly, real design principles that go beyond mechanical correctness.
Understanding this well is what separates a module that is merely functional from one that is genuinely pleasant to actually use.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550402730-357214373.png
blocks.alt: The Modules module, already covered mechanically, real design principles here

blocks.content: 2. Doing One Real Thing Well
A well-designed module does one real, coherent thing, and does it well, rather than attempting to handle every possible, tangentially-related concern at once.
A networking module handles networking, a database module handles the database, mixing unrelated real concerns into one module makes it genuinely harder to reuse.
This single-purpose focus is what makes a module genuinely composable, several focused modules combine more cleanly than one sprawling one.
This principle echoes good software design generally, worth recognizing as a real, transferable idea, not something unique to Terraform.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550405091-970654802.png
blocks.alt: One real, coherent thing, done well, rather than everything at once

blocks.content: 3. A Clean Interface, Hiding Complexity
Recall Reusable Modules, a clean interface, real inputs and outputs, hides internal complexity behind it, exactly the principle already introduced there.
A caller of a well-designed module should not need to understand its internal resource structure to use it correctly.
This is worth treating as a real, deliberate design goal, not something that simply happens automatically as a module is written.
Achieving this takes real, upfront thought about exactly which internal details genuinely need to be exposed, and which do not.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550406976-560506245.png
blocks.alt: A clean interface, recap, real internal complexity hidden deliberately behind it

blocks.content: 4. Sensible Defaults
Recall Default Values from the Variables module, sensible, real defaults mean most callers of a module need to supply genuinely little to use it correctly.
A module requiring a long list of required arguments, with no sensible defaults, is genuinely harder, and more frustrating, to actually adopt.
Choosing good, real defaults takes real, deliberate thought about the actual, common case a module is most likely to be used for.
This is precisely the same default-values principle already covered, applied here specifically to real module design.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550408932-723934627.png
blocks.alt: Most callers needing to supply genuinely little, thanks to real, sensible defaults

blocks.content: 5. Avoiding Over-Engineering
Exposing every possible internal option as a variable, just in case it is genuinely needed someday, is a real, common form of over-engineering worth avoiding.
This makes a module's real interface genuinely harder to understand, without necessarily corresponding to actual, real demand for that flexibility.
The more honest, practical approach adds a real, new variable only once an actual, genuine need for it arises.
This mirrors the same incremental, honest approach already covered for building a scoped IAM policy in the Security module.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550410758-5886461.png
blocks.alt: Genuine over-engineering, worth avoiding, exposing options with no real, actual demand

blocks.content: 6. A Real, Well-Designed Example
A genuinely well-designed VPC module exposes few, real inputs, a CIDR block, perhaps a name, with sensible defaults for nearly everything else.
Its internal resource structure, subnets, route tables, gateways, stays genuinely hidden behind that clean, minimal interface.
This is worth treating as a real, concrete illustration of every principle covered so far in this topic, brought together in one example.
Studying a real, well-regarded public module, covered in the Public Registry Modules topic, is a genuinely good way to see these principles applied in practice.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550412519-612132089.png
blocks.alt: Few real inputs, sensible defaults, a clean interface, every principle brought together

blocks.content: 7. Designing for Real Evolution
Recall Module Versioning, a well-designed module is built anticipating real, future change, new required inputs added as new major versions, not silently, breakingly.
This applies the semantic versioning discipline already covered directly to how a module's own interface is actually allowed to evolve over real time.
Designing with this in mind from the start avoids a real, painful situation later, needing to break every existing caller for one, small new feature.
This forward-looking discipline is what makes a module genuinely trustworthy for other real teams to depend on.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550414430-190771661.png
blocks.alt: Module versioning, already covered, applied directly to how a module evolves

blocks.content: 8. A Real, Common Mistake
A module trying to do genuinely everything at once, networking, compute, and monitoring, all bundled together, is a real, common design mistake.
This often starts innocently, convenient at first, but genuinely limits reuse, a team needing only networking still has to pull in everything else.
The honest fix is splitting an overly broad module into several, genuinely focused ones, each doing one real thing well.
Recognizing this pattern early, before a module grows too large to comfortably split, is genuinely worth the effort.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550416773-406283708.png
blocks.alt: A real, common mistake, trying to do genuinely everything in one, single module

9. Testing a Module in Isolation
A genuinely well-designed module should be testable on its own, applied against a real, disposable environment, without needing the entire, larger project around it.
A simple, real example configuration, living alongside a module purely for this purpose, is a genuinely worthwhile, practical addition.
This mirrors the same isolation principle already covered for testing a real state restructuring safely before touching production.
A module that only ever works as part of one, larger configuration is often a real sign its interface is not genuinely clean enough yet.

blocks.content: 10. Documenting a Module's Interface
A real README for a module, listing its inputs, outputs, and a short, real usage example, is worth exactly the same care as documentation covered for project structure.
This is especially genuinely important for a module intended for reuse, covered in Reusable Modules, across more than one real project or team.
A module's own variable and output descriptions, recall Terraform's support for these directly in variable and output blocks, are a real, built-in form of this documentation too.
Treating a module's interface as something genuinely worth documenting, not just something that happens to work, is a real mark of professional quality.

blocks.content: 11. When to Split vs Combine Modules
blocks.text: 11. When to Split vs Combine Modules

blocks.content: Deciding when to split one module into several, versus keeping related logic combined, is a real, practical judgment call worth revisiting as a module genuinely grows.
The real signal covered earlier, callers needing only part of a module's functionality, is the clearest, honest indicator it is genuinely time to split.
Combining too eagerly recreates the do-everything mistake already covered, splitting too eagerly creates unnecessary, real coordination overhead between tiny modules.
This mirrors the exact same honest granularity tradeoff already covered for state management, neither extreme is genuinely ideal.

["Split when callers genuinely need only part of a module's functionality.","Avoid combining too eagerly, recreating the do-everything mistake.","Avoid splitting too eagerly, creating unnecessary real coordination overhead."]
items: Split when callers genuinely need only part of a module's functionality.
Avoid combining too eagerly, recreating the do-everything mistake.
Avoid splitting too eagerly, creating unnecessary real coordination overhead.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A well-designed module does one real, coherent thing well, with a clean interface and sensible defaults hiding internal complexity.
Avoid over-engineering, exposing every possible option as a variable, and avoid a module trying to do genuinely everything at once.
Design for real, future evolution, a breaking interface change belongs in a new major version, exactly like semantic versioning already covered.
